extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate or beginning graduate students studying mathematical logic / computer science
extracted.subtask_description: Define the formal language of sentential (propositional) logic: specify symbols, formation rules (well-formed formulas), semantics via truth assignments, methods for checking tautologies/implication (truth tables), and a parsing algorithm ensuring unique decomposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal language specified in three parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe a formal language by specifying (1) the set of symbols (the alphabet), (2) the rules for forming grammatically correct finite sequences of symbols (well-formed formulas or wffs), and (3) the allowable translations between English (or informal language) and the formal language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first two parts (alphabet and formation rules) are purely syntactic; only the third part assigns meaning. Each part should be made explicit when defining a formal language. Examples: listing logical symbols and sentence symbols; giving formation rules like (¬ α), (α ∧ β); and indicating how sentence symbols map to declarative English sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alphabet / symbol set
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify the symbols that make up the alphabet (e.g., parentheses '(', ')', connectives ¬, ∧, ∨, →, ↔, and sentence symbols A1, A2, ...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State any constraints on symbols (the text requires that no symbol be a finite sequence of other symbols to ensure unique decomposition). Distinguish logical symbols (connectives and parentheses) from nonlogical/parameter sentence symbols whose translation can vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-formed formula (wff) formation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A wff is an expression built up from sentence symbols by finitely many applications of the formula-building operations: if α and β are wffs then (¬ α), (α ∧ β), (α ∨ β), (α → β), (α ↔ β) are wffs; every sentence symbol is a wff; and no other expressions are wffs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give the base cases and closure rules explicitly (the E¬, E∧, E∨, E→, E↔ equations in the text). Use these rules to decide syntactic well-formedness; examples illustrate valid and invalid expressions. Anti-pattern: treating arbitrary symbol sequences as wffs (e.g., ((→ A3).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction sequences and structural induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterize wffs via construction sequences: a finite sequence ε1,...,εn where each εi is either a sentence symbol, E¬(εj) for some earlier j, or E⊙(εj,εk) for some earlier j,k (⊙ a binary connective).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to justify the induction principle: any set S of wffs containing all sentence symbols and closed under the five formula-building operations equals the set of all wffs. Apply strong/structural induction on construction sequences to prove properties of wffs (e.g., counts of symbols).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parenthesis balance and proper-initial-segment property
rubrics_metrics.description: Every wff has the same number of left and right parentheses; any proper initial segment of a wff contains an excess of left parentheses (no proper initial segment is itself a wff).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These syntactic invariants are used to detect non-wffs and are central to parsing: a balanced prefix indicates a constituent boundary; an initial unbalanced-left prefix ensures uniqueness of constituent boundaries. Anti-pattern: omitting parentheses leads to ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parsing algorithm for wffs (uniqueness and error detection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure to decide whether an expression is a wff and to build its unique construction tree: (1) if all minimal vertices are sentence symbols halt; otherwise pick a minimal non-sentence expression; (2) first symbol must be '('; if second is '¬' handle as unary case; (3) otherwise, find smallest balanced nonempty α after '('; the next symbol must be a binary connective; remainder must be β) and create left/right child nodes; (4) unary case: remainder must be β) and create single child. Reject when required patterns fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The algorithm always halts (each step reduces expression length) and choices are forced by balance and Lemma 13B, proving the parse tree is unique. Error conditions: missing initial '(', improperly balanced substrings, missing principal connective, or unclosed parentheses — any such case causes rejection as non-wff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of decomposition / parse-tree
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the formula-building operations 'build up and never down' (each composed expression includes its constituents as contiguous segments), each wff has a unique way it was built, yielding a unique parse tree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Lemmas about balanced parentheses and proper initial segments to show constituent boundaries are forced; uniqueness underpins the existence and uniqueness of the extension of truth assignments to all wffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth assignments and extension to wffs (semantics for connectives)
rubrics_metrics.description: A truth assignment v for a set S of sentence symbols is a function v:S→{F,T}. It extends uniquely to v: Ŝ→{F,T} on all wffs built from S satisfying: (0) v(A)=v(A) for sentence symbols; (1) v((¬α)) = T iff v(α)=F; (2) v((α ∧ β)) = T iff v(α)=T and v(β)=T; (3) v((α ∨ β)) = T iff v(α)=T or v(β)=T (or both); (4) v((α → β)) = F iff v(α)=T and v(β)=F (i.e., false only when antecedent true and consequent false); (5) v((α ↔ β)) = T iff v(α)=v(β).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the truth-table (Table III) to make definitions explicit. Note vacuous truth of conditionals (if antecedent false then conditional true). Use structural/inductive proofs to show uniqueness/existence of the extension. Anti-pattern: trying to evaluate a wff under an assignment that doesn't include all its sentence symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of truth-value domain (two-valued vs multi-valued)
rubrics_metrics.description: The text commits to two-valued logic with truth values {F,T}, but notes alternatives (three-valued logic, 512-valued, continuum [0,1], or a complete Boolean algebra) are possible and sometimes interesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defining semantics, explicitly state the set of truth values; many semantic results depend on this choice. For introductory sentential logic, use {F,T} as standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of tautological implication, tautology, and equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Tautological implication: a set Γ of wffs tautologically implies τ (Γ |= τ) iff every truth assignment for the sentence symbols in Γ∪{τ} that satisfies every member of Γ also satisfies τ. Tautology: |= τ means every truth assignment satisfies τ (special case Γ=∅). Tautological equivalence: σ and τ are equivalent if σ |= τ and τ |= σ (equivalently |= (σ ↔ τ)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handle special cases: (a) If Γ is inconsistent (no assignment satisfies all members) then Γ |= τ for every τ (vacuous truth). (b) If Γ=∅, tautologies are those satisfied by every assignment. Use these precise semantic notions when proving logical consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth-table method for checking implication and tautology
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic procedure: list all 2^n truth assignments for the n sentence symbols occurring, compute truth values for the given formulas under each assignment (using truth-functional definitions), and check whether every assignment that satisfies the premises also satisfies the conclusion (or whether every assignment satisfies a given formula for tautology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct tables with one row per assignment and columns for subformulas. For small n this is feasible; for larger n reduce work by exploiting symmetries or case-splitting (e.g., short-circuit when a variable's value already forces the outcome). Anti-pattern: attempting full truth tables for large n without optimizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computational complexity warning (exponential blowup)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the full truth-table method to a wff with n sentence symbols requires 2^n rows; this grows exponentially and quickly becomes infeasible (example: n=80 gives 2^80 rows — astronomically large).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize practical limits of truth tables and motivate search for more efficient methods (e.g., proof systems, resolution, tableau, SAT solvers). The text notes the P vs NP question as related to whether substantially faster general methods exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selected tautologies and standard equivalences (laws to rely on)
rubrics_metrics.description: List of commonly used tautologies: associative and commutative laws for ∧, ∨, ↔; distributive laws; negation laws including double-negation and De Morgan’s; excluded middle (A ∨ ¬A); contradiction (¬(A ∧ ¬A)); contraposition ((A → B) ↔ (¬B → ¬A)); exportation (((A ∧ B) → C) ↔ (A → (B → C))).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these known equivalences to transform formulas, reduce truth-table size, or prove tautological equivalence. They serve as a toolkit for algebraic manipulation of wffs instead of brute-force checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution principle and duality
rubrics_metrics.description: If ϕ is a tautology then any substitution instance ϕ* (replace each An by some wff αn) is also a tautology. Duality: for wffs with only ∧, ∨, ¬, replacing ∧ with ∨, ∨ with ∧, and each sentence symbol by its negation yields α* tautologically equivalent to ¬α.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use substitution to generate new tautologies from known ones. Use duality to derive equivalences involving negations and to reason about complementary formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compactness theorem (semantic criterion for satisfiability)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an (possibly infinite) set Γ of wffs has the property that every finite subset Γ0 of Γ is satisfiable, then Γ itself is satisfiable (there exists a truth assignment satisfying every member of Γ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State as: if every finite subset of Γ is satisfiable then Γ is satisfiable. The text points to a topological proof (Tychonoff) and treats compactness as essential background for later results. Use compactness when reducing infinite problems to finite checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satisfaction, vacuity, and special-case reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Define 'v satisfies ϕ' as v(ϕ)=T. Recognize vacuous implications: Γ |= τ holds whenever Γ has no satisfying assignment. The empty set |= τ exactly when τ is a tautology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful in proofs and examples to consider vacuous cases explicitly (inconsistent premise sets and the empty premise set). Use small counterexample assignments to show non-implication.
